sections.title: Fats
sections.narration: 9.6 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 2.2 grams, which is a little heavy for a tuber food. Polyunsaturated fat is 2.8 grams, helping a little with useful unsaturated fat. Fat isn't the main job for tubers though.

sections.title: Carbs
sections.narration: 24 grams of carbs. Starch is 16 grams, giving some steady carb energy. However, the glycemic index is 74, which is really not the best for steady carb behaviour, and this does hurt the score for tubers. Sugar is 0.5 grams but that is to be expected from tubers. For tubers, carb quality decides a lot.

sections.title: Pros
sections.narration: The upsides first: easy freezer-side convenience. That makes them simple and convenient. Crisp texture can feel satisfying. That helps explain the snack appeal. Homemade versions can improve the health score a lot. Ingredients used matter of course, but not as much as simply leaving out all the additives used in prepackaged versions.

sections.title: Cons
sections.narration: The drawbacks next: still a processed fried snack. The original potato identity is not enough to save it. Cooking methods and preparation can impact a lot. Deep frying can push calories up to around 250 and add about 7 grams of fat. Easy to overeat as a side. Small pieces make casual portions creep up quickly.

closing.summary: Best bits are convenience, texture, and some starch energy. Weak spots are glycemic index, low potassium, and the processed fried format. Best for occasional comfort-food sides, not daily staple carbs. Essentially this convenience food format takes a basic tuber idea and just makes the nutrition tradeoff worse.
